disconnect_choice.menu:
The certificate arrived. What should this device do next?
    1) Continue - install it and proceed with the rotation
    2) Simulate a disconnect - the certificate arrived but was never written to disk (a crash or a dropped connection right here)
disconnect_choice.disconnecting: Simulating a disconnect: the certificate that just arrived is being discarded, not installed.
disconnect_choice.reconnected: Reconnected on the CURRENT certificate - the new one was never installed, so this is the only one this device still holds.
disconnect_choice.reasking: Asking again with the SAME certificate signing request - same key, same job. Watch the handler's logs for `redelivering` rather than a second signature.

cutover.proving: Proving the new certificate is authorized by publishing to {} ...
cutover.proved: Authorized publish with the new certificate succeeded.
cutover.connect_failed: The new certificate could not connect (reason_code={}). It was issued, but it is not usable - so the rotation stops here.
cutover.publish_refused: The new certificate connected but the broker REFUSED the publish: reason_code={}. The certificate works; its policy does not authorize this topic.
cutover.publish_failed: The new certificate could not publish: {}
cutover.rolled_back: Rolled back to the CURRENT certificate — it was never retired — and reported FAILED. The device stays online.

result.succeeded: Job execution reported SUCCEEDED. The backend may now retire the old certificate.
result.failed: Job execution reported FAILED. No certificate was retired, and the device keeps using its current certificate.
result.summary: Rotation complete for {}: new certificate {} is in use.

break_after_csr.exit: Breaking here on purpose, as requested by --break-after-csr. Certificate signing request sent for job execution {} and left unanswered - the execution stays IN_PROGRESS, phase=INITIATED. Re-run this same command WITHOUT --break-after-csr to pick it back up: a fresh process generates a new key pair and asks again, which is what makes the handler sign a second certificate (resigning) instead of re-delivering this one.

pause.prompt: Press Enter to let the device continue ...
pause.budget: Time budget: about {} of {} minutes left before AWS IoT Core marks this execution TIMED_OUT.
pause.disabled: No terminal input available - continuing without further pauses.
pause.not_a_terminal: Pausing was requested but this is not an interactive terminal; running straight through.
pause.exit: Stopped. The job execution was left exactly where it was paused; re-run this command to pick it back up.

job_taken.what: OBSERVE 1/3 - the job execution is now IN_PROGRESS. The device is holding here before it generates a key pair.
job_taken.console:
Console: AWS IoT console -> Manage -> Remote actions -> Jobs -> your job -> Job executions
           {}

overlap.what: OBSERVE 2/3 - the overlap window. The new certificate is signed, ACTIVE and attached, and the current one is still attached and working. The thing has TWO certificates right now, which is exactly why a failed rotation cannot lock the device out.
overlap.console:
Console: AWS IoT console -> Manage -> Things -> your thing -> Certificates
           {}
overlap.expect: Expect:  two principals listed. The new one ends in {}.

retired.what: OBSERVE 3/3 - the cutover succeeded, so the old certificate is being set INACTIVE. The retirement is event-driven, so give it a moment and re-run the command if it still shows ACTIVE. It is not deleted yet: retirement is deferred so a device that reappears late can still be recovered.
retired.console:
Console: AWS IoT console -> Security -> Certificates (the old one now shows Inactive)
           {}
retired.cli:
CLI:     Use the OTHER certificate id you saw at OBSERVE 2 - the one that is not the new certificate:
             aws iot describe-certificate --certificate-id <thatId> \
               --query "certificateDescription.status"   (expect: INACTIVE)
retired.scheduler:
CLI:     aws scheduler list-schedules --name-prefix ws-aws-iot-dm-adv-prov-revoke- \
               --query "Schedules[].[Name,State]"
             The one-time deletion timer. Its name ends with the first 16 characters of the retired certificate id.

cli.description: Run the device half of a backend-driven certificate rotation.
cli.telemetry_topic: Topic used to prove the new certificate is authorized
cli.request_rule: Name of the topic rule that receives the certificate signing request. The request is published over Basic Ingest ($aws/rules/<rule>/devices/<thing>/certificate/rotation/request) so it reaches the rules engine without a messaging charge. Must match the rule you created, or the publish is dropped and RuleNotFound is emitted
cli.job_timeout: Seconds to wait for a pending job execution
cli.cert_timeout: Seconds to wait for the signed certificate
cli.no_rollback: Do not fall back to the current certificate when the cutover fails
cli.connect_retries: Attempts to connect with the new certificate before giving up. An authorization failure (CONNACK NOT_AUTHORIZED) is never retried, because retrying cannot change it
cli.connect_backoff: Base seconds between connect attempts; doubles after each attempt
cli.pause: Pause at each observable step so you can inspect the job execution, the certificate overlap and the deferred retirement before continuing
cli.break_after_csr: Exit immediately after sending the certificate signing request, before waiting for the signed reply — a deterministic stand-in for a device that restarts in that gap. Re-run WITHOUT this flag afterwards: a fresh process generates a new key pair and asks again, which is what makes the handler sign a second certificate (`resigning`) instead of re-delivering the first one
cli.in_progress_timeout: Minutes the job allows an execution to stay IN_PROGRESS; used to warn how long you may pause before the execution is marked TIMED_OUT
